nameStory: This beetle earned its 'emerald' name from its brilliant metallic green body that shimmers like a precious gem in sunlight. The 'ash borer' part tells you exactly what trouble it causes - the larvae tunnel through ash tree bark, creating the characteristic D-shaped holes that give away their presence. It belongs to the jewel beetle family, named for their stunning metallic colors that look like living jewelry.
description: The emerald ash borer is a small, brilliantly metallic green beetle about half an inch long that has become one of New England's most destructive invasive insects. Originally from Asia, this jewel beetle exclusively attacks ash trees, where females lay eggs in bark crevices and larvae tunnel underneath the bark. Adult beetles emerge after one to two years, leaving behind distinctive D-shaped exit holes. While beautiful to look at, this species has killed millions of ash trees across North America since its introduction.

idTips.label: Metallic Green Body
idTips.description: Brilliant emerald green color with a metallic sheen that catches light like polished metal - no other common beetle in New England has quite this intense green shine

idTips.label: D-shaped Exit Holes
idTips.description: Look for distinctive D-shaped holes about 1/8 inch across in ash tree bark - these are exit holes left by emerging adults and feel smooth to the touch around the edges

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: About half an inch long with a narrow, elongated body typical of jewel beetles - roughly the size of a large grain of rice but much more cylindrical

idTips.label: S-shaped Larval Galleries
idTips.description: Under loose ash bark, you'll find serpentine S-shaped tunnels packed with sawdust-like material that feels gritty between your fingers

idTips.label: Host Tree Association
idTips.description: Only found on ash trees (look for opposite branching and compound leaves with 5-9 leaflets) - if it's not an ash tree, it's not emerald ash borer

habitat: Found exclusively on ash trees throughout New England's forests, parks, and residential areas. Look for them in both wet lowland areas where black ash grows and drier upland sites with white and green ash. They prefer stressed or weakened trees but will attack healthy ash trees as populations build up.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from D-shaped holes in late spring, leaving fresh exit holes in ash bark. Look for the bright green beetles on ash foliage during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.summer: Peak adult activity occurs in summer when beetles are mating and females are laying eggs in bark crevices. Fresh exit holes and adult beetles are most commonly observed during this season.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down, but D-shaped exit holes remain visible. This is a good time to examine ash trees for damage signs without the distraction of other insect activity.
seasonality.winter: Larvae are developing under the bark in their tunnels. Look for woodpecker damage on ash trees - these birds often target EAB larvae, creating distinctive rectangular holes in the bark.

funFact: Woodpeckers have become unexpected allies in the fight against emerald ash borer - they can detect the larvae moving under bark and will strip large sections of bark off infested trees, creating a 'blonding' effect that makes damaged ash trees visible from hundreds of yards away.
confusionNotes: The brilliant metallic green color is fairly distinctive, but other jewel beetles can be confused with EAB. Remember the simple rule: if it's not on an ash tree, it's not emerald ash borer - this species is completely host-specific to ash trees.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beautiful appearance, EAB is considered one of the most destructive forest pests ever introduced to North America. Many states have quarantine regulations restricting the movement of ash wood and nursery stock to slow its spread. The beetle was likely introduced through wooden shipping materials from Asia.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives the red-necked cane borer (which attacks berry canes and has a reddish thorax) and other Agrilus species that often have bronze or copper coloring, emerald ash borer is distinctly emerald green all over. The combination of bright green metallic color and exclusive association with ash trees makes it unique among New England's Agrilus beetles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its notorious relative the Emerald Ash Borer which is uniformly bright green and attacks ash trees, the red-necked cane borer has that distinctive reddish thorax and targets berry canes.

Compared to its relatives, the Blue-green Jewel Beetle is distinguished by its blue-green coloration versus the Red-necked Cane Borer's reddish neck area and the Emerald Ash Borer's brighter emerald-green color.
